claim: Twenty healthy participants (13 females; mean age: 28 years; age range: 20–46) took part in an fMRI and a behavioral experiment.
source: Twenty healthy participants (13 females; mean age: 28 years; age range: 20–46) took part in an fMRI and a behavioral experiment carried out at the Combined Universities Brain Imaging Centre (CUBIC) at Royal Holloway University of London (RHUL).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number, demographics, and participation details of the study participants.

claim: The experiment was approved by the ethics committee at the Department of Psychology, RHUL (REF 2015/088).
source: The experiment was approved by the ethics committee at the Department of Psychology, RHUL (REF 2015/088).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the ethics approval reference.

claim: All participants were right-handed with normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no history of neurological or psychiatric disease.
source: All participants were right-handed with normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no history of neurological or psychiatric disease.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the inclusion criteria for participants.

claim: All participants but one (RT, one of the authors) were naïve to the purpose of the study.
source: All participants but one (RT, one of the authors) were naïve to the purpose of the study.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states participant awareness of study purpose.

claim: The semantic dissimilarity structure was best captured by patterns of activation in the lateral occipitotemporal cortex (LOTC).
source: Using multiple regression representational similarity analysis of fMRI data, in which we accounted for variability due to major action components (body parts, scenes, movements, objects, sociality, transitivity) and three control models (distance between observer and actor, number of people, HMAX-C1), we found that the semantic dissimilarity structure was best captured by patterns of activation in the lateral occipitotemporal cortex (LOTC).
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the main finding from the multiple regression RSA analysis.

claim: The organization of observed actions in the LOTC resembles the organizing principles used by participants to classify actions behaviorally.
source: Together, our results demonstrate that the organization of observed actions in the LOTC resembles the organizing principles used by participants to classify actions behaviorally, in line with the view that this region is crucial for accessing the meaning of actions.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this conclusion based on the study results.

claim: LOTC is crucial for accessing the meaning of actions.
source: Together, our results demonstrate that the organization of observed actions in the LOTC resembles the organizing principles used by participants to classify actions behaviorally, in line with the view that this region is crucial for accessing the meaning of actions.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this interpretation of the results.

claim: There exists a widespread network of fronto-parietal regions involved in action control and recognition, with a preference along the dorso-medial stream and the dorso-lateral stream for reaching and grasping movements, respectively.
source: This literature revealed a widespread network of fronto-parietal regions, with a preference along the dorso-medial stream and the dorso-lateral stream for reaching and grasping movements, respectively (for reviews see e.g. Culham and Valyear, 2006; Rizzolatti and Matelli, 2003; Turella and Lingnau, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous reviews to support this claim about neural organization.

claim: Less is known regarding the organization of more complex actions.
source: Less is known regarding the organization of more complex actions (for exceptions, see Abdollahi et al., 2013; Jastorff et al., 2010; Wurm et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this gap in knowledge while citing some exceptions.

claim: Higher-level semantic categories often covary with more basic action components such as body parts, movement kinematics, and objects.
source: Note that higher-level semantic categories often covary with more basic action components (such as body parts, movement kinematics, and objects) of perceived action scenes.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this relationship between semantic categories and action components.

claim: Locomotion actions tend to involve the legs, consist of repetitive movements, can involve vehicles such as a bike and often take place outdoors.
source: As an example, locomotion actions tend to involve the legs, consist of repetitive movements, can involve vehicles such as a bike and often take place outdoors, whereas communicative actions often involve mouth/lip movements, consist of small movements, can involve objects such as a mobile phone, and can take place in a variety of different scenes.
evidence: The manuscript provides this as an explicit example of how semantic categories covary with action components.

claim: Communicative actions often involve mouth/lip movements, consist of small movements, can involve objects such as a mobile phone, and can take place in a variety of different scenes.
source: As an example, locomotion actions tend to involve the legs, consist of repetitive movements, can involve vehicles such as a bike and often take place outdoors, whereas communicative actions often involve mouth/lip movements, consist of small movements, can involve objects such as a mobile phone, and can take place in a variety of different scenes.
evidence: The manuscript provides this as an explicit example of how semantic categories covary with action components.

claim: It is possible to distinguish between different actions on the basis of patterns of brain activation in the lateral occipito-temporal cortex (LOTC), the inferior parietal lobe (IPL) and the ventral premotor cortex (PMv).
source: The general results that emerged from these studies is that it is possible to distinguish between different actions on the basis of patterns of brain activation in the lateral occipito-temporal cortex (LOTC), the inferior parietal lobe (IPL) and the ventral premotor cortex (PMv).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from previous MVPA studies cited in the text.

claim: LOTC has been shown to contain action-related object properties.
source: In line with this view, LOTC has been shown to contain action-related object properties (Bracci and Peelen, 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study to support this claim.

claim: LOTC and IPL, but not the PMv, showed a generalization across the way in which actions were performed.
source: LOTC and IPL, but not the PMv, furthermore showed a generalization across the way in which these actions were performed (e.g. performing the same action with different kinematics), suggesting that these areas represent actions at more general levels and thus possibly the meaning of the actions (Wurm and Lingnau, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study to support this claim.

claim: LOTC and IPL represent actions at more general levels and thus possibly the meaning of the actions.
source: LOTC and IPL, but not the PMv, furthermore showed a generalization across the way in which these actions were performed (e.g. performing the same action with different kinematics), suggesting that these areas represent actions at more general levels and thus possibly the meaning of the actions (Wurm and Lingnau, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript presents this as an inference from cited research.

claim: The individual RDMs significantly correlated with the average RDM of the remaining participants for the semantic task (mean leave-one-subject-out correlation coefficient: 0.61, min: 0.46, max: 0.78).
source: We found significant (all p-values were smaller than p<0.0001 and survived false discovery rate correction) inter-observer correlations, that is the individual RDMs significantly correlated with the average RDM of the remaining participants (mean leave-one-subject-out correlation coefficient: 0.61, min individual correlation coefficient: 0.46, max individual correlation coefficient: 0.78), suggesting that the participants' arrangements were reliable and based on comparable principles.
evidence: The manuscript reports specific statistical results from the behavioral experiment.

claim: The participants' arrangements in the semantic task were reliable and based on comparable principles.
source: We found significant (all p-values were smaller than p<0.0001 and survived false discovery rate correction) inter-observer correlations, that is the individual RDMs significantly correlated with the average RDM of the remaining participants (mean leave-one-subject-out correlation coefficient: 0.61, min individual correlation coefficient: 0.46, max individual correlation coefficient: 0.78), suggesting that the participants' arrangements were reliable and based on comparable principles.
evidence: The manuscript infers reliability from the significant inter-observer correlations.

claim: The optimal number of clusters for the semantic task was six.
source: A Silhouette analysis (see Materials and methods and Figure 3—figure supplement 1) revealed that the optimal number of clusters for the semantic task was six.
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of the Silhouette analysis and references the corresponding figure.

claim: The first three components of the PCA account for the largest amount of variance in the semantic task.
source: As can be seen in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, the first three components account for the largest amount of variance.
evidence: The manuscript references a figure showing the PCA results.

claim: The semantic task revealed clusters related to locomotion (e.g. biking, running), social/communicative actions (e.g. handshaking, talking on the phone), leisure-related actions (e.g. painting, reading), food-related actions (e.g. eating, drinking), and cleaning-related actions (e.g. showering, washing the dishes).
source: The analysis revealed clusters related to locomotion (e.g. biking, running), social/communicative actions (e.g. handshaking, talking on the phone), leisure-related actions (e.g. painting, reading), food-related actions (e.g. eating, drinking), and cleaning-related actions (e.g. showering, washing the dishes).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the clusters identified from the K-means analysis.

claim: Standard RSA using the semantic model revealed significant clusters in bilateral LOTC extending ventrally into inferior temporal cortex, bilateral posterior intraparietal sulcus (pIPS), and bilateral inferior frontal gyrus/ventral premotor cortex.
source: We identified significant clusters in bilateral LOTC extending ventrally into inferior temporal cortex, bilateral posterior intraparietal sulcus (pIPS), and bilateral inferior frontal gyrus/ventral premotor cortex (Figure 4, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of the standard RSA and references the corresponding figure and supplementary file.

claim: The semantic model explained significant amounts of variance over and above the six models for the different action components and the three control models in the left anterior LOTC at the junction to the posterior middle temporal gyrus.
source: As can be seen in Figure 6, the semantic model explained significant amounts of variance over and above the six models for the different action components and the three control models in the left anterior LOTC at the junction to the posterior middle temporal gyrus (see also Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of the multiple regression RSA and references the corresponding figures.

claim: All models except the sociality and the scene model revealed significant clusters in the multiple regression RSA.
source: All models except the sociality and the scene model revealed significant clusters (see Supplementary file 2 for details).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states which models showed significant results.

claim: The body model revealed a cluster predominantly in the left angular gyrus, slightly more dorsal than the cluster revealed by the semantic model, and the right pMTG.
source: For the body model (Figure 7A), the cluster was obtained predominantly in the left angular gyrus, slightly more dorsal than the cluster revealed by the semantic model, and the right pMTG.
evidence: The manuscript describes the location of clusters revealed by the body model and references the corresponding figure.

claim: The cluster revealed by the body model in the left hemisphere was more dorsal than Extrastriate Body Area (EBA).
source: Note that the cluster revealed by the body model in the left hemisphere was more dorsal than Extrastriate Body Area (EBA) (Downing et al., 2001) (for a comparison with coordinates revealed by previous studies that used a functional localizer to identify EBA, see Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly compares the location of the cluster to EBA and references a figure showing this comparison.

claim: The movement model revealed clusters in the left SPL, the left inferior occipital gyrus (posterior to the cluster revealed by the semantic model) and the right MTG.
source: The movement model revealed clusters in the left SPL, the left inferior occipital gyrus (posterior to the cluster revealed by the semantic model) and the right MTG (Figure 7B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the location of clusters revealed by the movement model and references the corresponding figure.

claim: The object model explained variance in the right intraparietal sulcus area 1 (IPS1) and the left fusiform gyrus area.
source: The object model explained variance in the right intraparietal sulcus area 1 (IPS1; Hagler et al., 2007) and the left fusiform gyrus area (Figure 7C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the location of clusters revealed by the object model and references the corresponding figure.

claim: The transitivity model revealed a small cluster in the left inferior occipital gyrus, posterior to the cluster revealed by the semantic cluster.
source: The transitivity model revealed a small cluster in the left inferior occipital gyrus, posterior to the cluster revealed by the semantic cluster (Figure 7D).
evidence: The manuscript describes the location of the cluster revealed by the transitivity model and references the corresponding figure.

claim: The HMAX-C1 model revealed clusters in the calcarine cortex (left hemisphere), the right occipital fusiform gyrus, the right inferior occipital gyrus, the right lingual gyrus and the left fusiform gyrus.
source: The HMAX-C1 model revealed clusters (distinct from the cluster revealed by the semantic model) in the calcarine cortex (left hemisphere), the right occipital fusiform gyrus, the right inferior occipital gyrus, the right lingual gyrus and the left fusiform gyrus (Figure 7G and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript describes the location of clusters revealed by the HMAX-C1 model and references the corresponding figure.

claim: The obtained RSA results are unlikely to be due to low-level features of the images used.
source: Note that the obtained RSA results are unlikely to be due to some low-level features of the images we used.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on the experimental design and control analyses.

claim: A substantial amount of variability was introduced for each of the 28 actions, using different exemplars in which the actor, the viewpoint, the background/scene, and the object were varied.
source: First, to minimize the risk that results could be driven by trivial pixel-wise perceptual similarities, we introduced a substantial amount of variability for each of the 28 actions, using different exemplars in which we varied the actor, the viewpoint, the background/scene (e.g. kitchen A vs kitchen B), and the object (for actions that involved one).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the experimental design to control for low-level features.

claim: Three control models (distance, one vs two people, HMAX-C1) were included in the multiple regression analysis to account for low-level perceptual similarities.
source: Second, as described above, to account for low-level perceptual similarities, we included three control models (distance, one vs two people, HMAX-C1) in the multiple regression analysis.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the inclusion of control models in the analysis.

claim: The semantic model is the model that best correlates with the neural RDM in the left LOTC.
source: The bar plot confirmed that the semantic model is the model that best correlates with the neural RDM (shown in Figure 8B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of the correlation analysis and references the corresponding figure.

claim: The averaged correlations between model RDMs and neural RDMs in the LOTC were quite low (semantic model: 0.0645, distance model: 0.0608, 1vs2People: 0.0563; all other models < 0.05).
source: Note that the averaged correlations were quite low (semantic model: 0.0645, distance model: 0.0608, 1vs2People: 0.0563; all other models < 0.05), in line with a number of previous studies (e.g. Bracci and Op de Beeck, 2016; Magri et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific correlation values and cites previous studies showing similar results.

claim: The organization of the neural multidimensional patterns associated with each action in the LOTC resembles the clustering organization observed for the behavioral semantic task.
source: As shown in Figure 8C, the organization of the neural multidimensional patters associated with each action indeed resembles the clustering organization we observed for the behavioral semantic task (see Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation based on the MDS analysis and references the corresponding figures.

claim: Inverse MDS identified a number of clusters emerging in the arrangement of actions according to their meaning that were relatively stable across participants.
source: Using inverse MDS (Kriegeskorte and Mur, 2012), we identified a number of clusters emerging in the arrangement of actions according to their meaning that were relatively stable across participants.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main finding from the behavioral experiment.

claim: The semantic similarity structure of observed actions was best captured in the patterns of activation in the left LOTC using multiple regression RSA.
source: Using multiple regression RSA (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008a), we showed that this semantic similarity structure of observed actions was best captured in the patterns of activation in the left LOTC.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main finding from the fMRI experiment.

claim: PCA suggested that the five categories revealed in the behavioral experiment appear to be organized along three main components that together explained around 78% of the observed variance.
source: PCA suggested that the five categories revealed in the behavioral experiment appear to be organized along three main components that together explained around 78% of the observed variance.
evidence: The manuscript reports the result of the PCA analysis.

claim: Clusters corresponding to semantic categories along the first principal component differed with respect to the type of change induced by the action (negative side: change of location, positive side: change of external/physical state, middle: change of internal/mental state).
source: Whereas neither the PCA nor the k-means clustering provides objective labels of the main dimensions that might underlie the organization of actions into categories, it appears that clusters corresponding to semantic categories along the first principal component differed with respect to the type of change induced by the action (negative side of component 1: change of location, positive side of component 1: change of external/physical state, middle: change of internal/mental state).
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the first principal component based on the data.

claim: The second component seemed to distinguish actions that fulfil basic (or physiological) needs and actions that fulfil higher (social belonging, self-fulfillment) needs.
source: The second component seemed to distinguish actions that fulfil basic (or physiological) needs such as eating, drinking, cutting, or getting from one place to the other, and actions that fulfil higher (social belonging, self-fulfillment) needs such as hugging, talking to someone, reading, listening to music).
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the second principal component based on the data.

claim: The distinction along the second component shows some similarity with Maslow's hierarchy structure of needs.
source: Interestingly, this distinction shows some similarity with Maslow's hierarchy structure of needs (Maslow, 1943).
evidence: The manuscript draws a comparison to Maslow's theory and cites the original work.

claim: The third component might capture the degree to which an action is directed towards another person or not.
source: The third component might capture the degree to which an action is directed towards another person (hugging, holding hands, talking, etc.) or not (running, swimming, playing video games, reading).
evidence: The manuscript provides an interpretation of the third principal component based on the data.

claim: Watson and Buxbaum (2014) found that the two components that best explained the variability of their ratings of tool-related actions were related to 'hand configuration' and 'magnitude of arm movement'.
source: Using ratings of the use of tools depicted as static images, Watson and Buxbaum (2014) found that the two components that best explained the variability of their ratings of tool-related actions were related to 'hand configuration' and 'magnitude of arm movement'.
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study on the organization of tool-related actions.

claim: Based on the examination of the relationship between verb meaning and verb behavior, authors including Talmy (1985), Levin (1993), and Pinker (1989) aimed to reveal the underlying semantic structure of verbs.
source: As an example, based on the examination of the relationship between verb meaning (e.g. to break, to appear) and verb behavior (e.g. whether or not a verb can be used transitively), a number of authors including Talmy (1985), Levin (1993), and Pinker (1989) aimed to reveal the underlying semantic structure of verbs (for related work on the use of semantic feature production norms see for example Vinson and Vigliocco, 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous linguistic research on verb semantics.

claim: Semantic categories proposed by Levin (1993) include change of location, communication, cooking, and change of state, which show similarities to the action categories revealed in the current study.
source: The latter include, but are not limited to, change of location, communication, cooking, and change of state, which show similarities to the action categories locomotion, communicative actions, food-related actions and cleaning-related actions revealed in the current study.
evidence: The manuscript compares the current findings to previous linguistic research.

claim: It is likely that there exist action categories that can be revealed by visual stimuli but not by language, and vice versa.
source: Whereas it is not surprising that action categories revealed on the basis of visual stimuli to some degree resemble semantic fields derived from cross-linguistic comparisons, it is likely that there exist action categories that can be revealed by visual stimuli but not by language, and vice versa (see also Vinson and Vigliocco, 2008, and Watson and Buxbaum, 2014, for related discussions on this topic).
evidence: The manuscript speculates about differences between visual and linguistic action representations and cites related discussions.

claim: Standard RSA observed a significant correlation between the semantic model and the pattern of fMRI data in regions of the action observation network, which broadly includes the LOTC, IPL, premotor and inferior frontal cortex.
source: To identify brain regions that encoded the similarity patterns revealed by the behavioral experiment, we conducted a searchlight-based RSA. We observed a significant correlation between the semantic model and the pattern of fMRI data in regions of the so-called action observation network (Caspers et al., 2010), which broadly includes the LOTC, IPL, premotor and inferior frontal cortex.
evidence: The manuscript reports the results of the standard RSA and cites a previous study defining the action observation network.

claim: Only the left LOTC contains action information as predicted by the semantic model over and above the remaining models in the multiple regression RSA.
source: Using multiple regression RSA, we found that only the left LOTC contains action information as predicted by the semantic model over and above the remaining models.
evidence: The manuscript reports the main finding from the multiple regression RSA.

claim: It has been demonstrated that it is possible to discriminate between observed actions based on the patterns of activation in the LOTC, generalizing across objects and kinematics.
source: In line with these results, it has been demonstrated that it is possible to discriminate between observed actions based on the patterns of activation in the LOTC, generalizing across objects and kinematics (Wurm et al., 2016), and at different levels of abstraction (Wurm and Lingnau, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies supporting the current findings.

claim: Studies using semantic tasks on actions using verbal stimuli or action classification across videos and written sentences tend to recruit anterior portions of the left LOTC.
source: Interestingly, studies using semantic tasks on actions using verbal stimuli (Watson et al., 2013) or action classification across videos and written sentences (Wurm and Caramazza, 2019a) tend to recruit anterior portions of the left LOTC.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies showing activation in anterior LOTC for verbal action tasks.

claim: Studies using static pictures or videos depicting actions find LOTC bilaterally and more posteriorly, closer to the cluster in the MOG identified in the current study.
source: By contrast, studies using static pictures (Hafri et al., 2017) or videos depicting actions (Hafri et al., 2017; Wurm et al., 2017; Wurm et al., 2016; Wurm and Lingnau, 2015) find LOTC bilaterally and more posteriorly, closer to the cluster in the MOG identified in the current study.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies showing activation in posterior LOTC for visual action tasks.

claim: Hafri et al. (2017) found a far more widespread network of areas decoding actions depicted by videos in comparison to static pictures.
source: Note that a previous study by Hafri et al. (2017), directly comparing areas in which it is possible to decode between actions depicted by static pictures and by dynamic videos, found a far more widespread network of areas decoding actions depicted by videos in comparison to static pictures.
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study comparing static and dynamic action stimuli.

claim: Hafri et al. (2017) demonstrated that it is possible to decode actions across stimulus format in the posterior LOTC.
source: At the same time, Hafri et al. (2017) demonstrated that it is possible to decode actions across stimulus format in the posterior LOTC, in line with the view that action-related representations in this area does not necessarily require visual motion.
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study showing cross-format decoding in LOTC.

claim: The LOTC captures semantic aspects of actions at higher-order visual levels, whereas anterior portions of the left LOTC might capture these aspects at stimulus-independent or verbal levels of representation.
source: Together, our findings suggest that this area captures semantic aspects of actions at higher-order visual levels, whereas anterior portions of the left LOTC might capture these aspects at stimulus-independent or verbal levels of representation (see also Lingnau and Downing, 2015 and Papeo et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript proposes this interpretation based on the current findings and cites related work.

claim: The LOTC has been shown to be sensitive to categorical action distinctions, such as whether they are directed towards persons or objects.
source: The LOTC has been shown to be sensitive to categorical action distinctions, such as whether they are directed towards persons or objects (Wurm et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study showing categorical distinctions in LOTC.

claim: The results obtained for the transitivity model are in line with the results reported by Wurm et al. (2017) and Wurm and Caramazza (2019b).
source: The results obtained for the transitivity model are in line with the results reported by Wurm et al. (2017) and Wurm and Caramazza (2019b), whereas we failed to obtain reliable results for the sociality model.
evidence: The manuscript compares the current findings to previous studies.

claim: The current study failed to obtain reliable results for the sociality model.
source: The results obtained for the transitivity model are in line with the results reported by Wurm et al. (2017) and Wurm and Caramazza (2019b), whereas we failed to obtain reliable results for the sociality model.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this negative result.

claim: Only a small number of actions were directed towards another person, and these actions co-varied with the presence of another person, which was captured by the 1 vs 2 people model.
source: Note, however, that the current study was not designed to test this model. In particular, only a small number of actions were directed towards another person, and these actions co-varied with the presence of another person, which was captured by the 1 vs 2 people model (which showed comparable results to those obtained for the sociality model in the study by Wurm et al., 2017; see also Wurm and Caramazza, 2019b for an experimental segregation of sociality and 1 vs. 2 people models).
evidence: The manuscript explains the lack of results for the sociality model and cites related work.

claim: The LOTC hosts a variety of different, partially overlapping representations of action components that are likely to be integrated flexibly according to task demands.
source: Together, the results of the multiple regression RSA obtained for the different models are in line with the view that the LOTC hosts a variety of different, partially overlapping representations of action components that are likely to be integrated flexibly according to task demands (see also Lingnau and Downing, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript proposes this interpretation based on the current findings and cites related work.

claim: Multiple, possibly overlapping basic dimensions have been proposed to underlie the organization of action components within the LOTC, among them the input modality (visual versus non-visual), the presence and orientation of a person, and the directedness of actions toward persons or other targets.
source: Multiple, possibly overlapping basic dimensions have been proposed to underlie the organization of these different action components within the LOTC, among them the input modality (visual versus non-visual; Lingnau and Downing, 2015; Papeo et al., 2019), the presence and orientation of a person, and the directedness of actions toward persons or other targets (Wurm et al., 2017; Wurm and Caramazza, 2019b).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes proposed organizational dimensions and cites relevant studies.

claim: The results obtained in the IPL and the precentral gyrus for the semantic model revealed by the standard RSA was due to some combination of the models accounted for in the multiple regression RSA.
source: This observation suggests that the results obtained in the IPL and the precentral gyrus for the semantic model revealed by the standard RSA was due to some combination of the models accounted for in the multiple regression RSA, even if no individual model alone revealed a cluster in these two regions that survived corrections for multiple comparisons.
evidence: The manuscript infers this explanation from the difference between standard and multiple regression RSA results.

claim: The LOTC has been demonstrated to represent the similarity structure of object categories.
source: In line with the results of the multiple regression-based RSA, the LOTC has been demonstrated to represent the similarity structure of object categories (Bracci and Op de Beeck, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study showing similar findings in the object domain.

claim: Salient distinctions at the behavioral and neural level have been found between animate and inanimate objects.
source: Regarding the results of the cluster analysis, salient distinctions at the behavioral and neural level have been found between animate and inanimate objects (for example Kriegeskorte et al., 2008b; Chao et al., 1999; Caramazza and Shelton, 1998) which have been further segregated into human and nonhuman objects (Mur et al., 2013), and manipulable and non-manipulable objects (Mecklinger et al., 2002), respectively.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on object categorization.

claim: The division between animate and inanimate objects has been suggested to have a special status, likely due to evolutionary pressures that favored fast and accurate recognition of animals.
source: The division between animate and inanimate objects, supported by neuropsychological, behavioral and neuroimaging findings, has been suggested to have a special status, likely due to evolutionary pressures that favored fast and accurate recognition of animals (Caramazza and Shelton, 1998; Mur et al., 2013; New et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies proposing an evolutionary explanation for the animate/inanimate distinction.

claim: Similar evolutionary mechanisms might have produced the distinction between actions belonging to different categories, such as locomotion, food-related actions and communicative actions.
source: We conjecture that similar evolutionary mechanisms might have produced the distinction between actions belonging to different categories, such as locomotion (which might indicate the approach of an enemy), food-related actions (which might be critical for survival) and communicative actions (critical for survival within a group).
evidence: The manuscript speculates about evolutionary explanations for action categorization.

claim: The LOTC plays a critical role in accessing the meaning of actions beyond the mere perceptual processing of action-relevant components.
source: Together, our results support the view that the LOTC plays a critical role in accessing the meaning of actions beyond the mere perceptual processing of action-relevant components.
evidence: The manuscript states this as the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Participants sat in front of a monitor (LCD 16.2 × 19.2 inches; distance 60 cm) during the inverse multidimensional scaling experiment.
source: Participants sat in front of a monitor (LCD 16.2 × 19.2 inches; distance 60 cm).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the experimental setup.

claim: In trial 1 of the inverse MDS experiment, all action images appeared on the screen in a circular arrangement with the order of actions randomly selected.
source: In trial 1, all action images (one exemplar per action) appeared on the screen in a circular arrangement (with the order of actions randomly selected; see Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the first trial of the inverse MDS experiment and references the corresponding figure.

claim: Participants were given 15 minutes in total to complete the inverse MDS task.
source: Participants were given 15 minutes in total to complete the task.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the time limit for the task.

claim: An online survey using Google Forms was carried out to identify actions that are considered common by a large sample of people.
source: To this aim, we initially carried out an online survey using Google Forms. The aim of the survey was to identify actions that are considered common by a large sample of people.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the initial stimulus selection procedure.

claim: 36 participants (different from those that took part in the fMRI study) were asked to spontaneously write down all the actions that came to their mind within 10 min.
source: We thus asked 36 participants (different from those that took part in the fMRI study) to spontaneously write down all the actions that came to their mind within 10 min that they or other people are likely to do or observe.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the online survey procedure.

claim: Actions were selected if they were mentioned by at least 20% of the participants in the online survey.
source: Actions were selected if they were mentioned by at least 20% of the participants.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the selection criterion for actions.

claim: In total, 37 actions were identified from the online survey.
source: In total, we identified 37 actions (see Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of actions identified.

claim: To maximize perceptual variability within each action, the actors, the scene, and perspectives were varied, for a total of 12 exemplars per action.
source: To maximize perceptual variability within each action, and thus to minimize low-level feature differences between actions, we varied the actors (2), the scene (2) and perspectives (3), for a total of 12 exemplars per action.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the stimulus creation procedure.

claim: Exemplars for the action 'swimming' were collected from the Internet because of the difficulties in taking photos in a public swimming pool.
source: Exemplars for the action 'swimming' were collected from the Internet because of the difficulties in taking photos in a public swimming pool.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this exception in the stimulus creation procedure.

claim: The final number of actions chosen for the main experiment was 28.
source: Therefore, the final number of actions chosen for the main experiment was 28 (see Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the final number of actions used.

claim: Static images were used instead of videos of actions to avoid systematic differences between conditions based on the kinematic profiles of videos and because static stimuli are more suitable for the inverse MDS experiment.
source: Note that we decided to use static images instead of videos of actions for two reasons. First of all, we wished to avoid systematic differences between conditions based on the kinematic profiles of videos of actions. Second, we aimed to use stimuli that are suitable both for the fMRI experiment and for the inverse MDS experiment. We considered static stimuli more suitable for the latter, given that the participant had to judge the similarity of a large set of actions simultaneously.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly explains the rationale for using static images.

source: For the acquisition of the functional images, we used a T2*-weighted gradient EPI sequence. claim: Significant inter-observer correlations were found for all behavioral models (semantic, body, scene, movement, object).
source: We found significant (all p-values were smaller than p<0.0001 and survived false discovery rate correction) inter-observer correlations, that is the individual RDMs significantly correlated with the average RDMs of the remaining participants (mean leave-one-subject-out correlation coefficients [min – max individual correlation coefficients]; semantic model: 0.61 [0.46–0.78], body model: 0.57 [0.31–0.70]; scene model: 0.63 [0.40–0.78]; movement model: 0.47 [0.26–0.67]; object model: 0.51 [0.22–0.71].
evidence: The manuscript reports specific statistical results for all behavioral models.

claim: To construct RDMs for the sociality and the transitivity models, an online experiment was conducted using Qualtrics and Amazon Mechanical Turk in which N = 20 participants judged the sociality and transitivity of each action on a Likert scale.
source: To construct RDMs for the sociality and the transitivity models (Wurm et al., 2017), we conducted an online experiment using Qualtrics and Amazon Mechanical Turn in which we asked a separate group of N = 20 participants to judge on a Likert scale (1: not at all; 7: very much) the sociality (i.e. the interaction between the actors involved) and transitivity (i.e. the use of an object) of each action.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the procedure for constructing these models and cites related work.

source: To construct the RDM for the distance model, we asked another group of N = 20 participants to judge the distance (1: within reaching distance; 2: not within reaching distance, but <= 3 meters, 3:>3 meters) from the observer at which each action takes place.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the procedure for constructing the distance model.

source: The model controlling for the number of people depicted in the action was constructed by coding one person involved as 0 and two people involved as 1.

source: The HMAX-C1 model (Serre et al., 2007) was derived similarly to Connolly et al.
